lead: A capacitor microphone and a capacitive pressure sensor use the same trick. A thin diaphragm is one plate of a capacitor. Sound or fluid pressure pushes the diaphragm, the gap changes, the capacitance changes, and a circuit turns that into a voltage. The microphone serves speech, music and noise measurement. The pressure sensor serves low-pressure, differential and flow measurements, as in ventilators and lung-function equipment. The change is tiny, so the amplifier and wiring matter as much as the plates.
prereq: You need: capacitive transducers: types and signal conditioning for C = ε₀A/d and charge-to-voltage conversion.

sections.h3: Capacitor microphone: how sound moves a plate

blocks.text: A capacitor microphone, also called a condenser microphone in some syllabi, has a thin metallised plastic or metal diaphragm. The diaphragm is one plate. A fixed back plate is the other. The air gap between them is d. Sound pressure pushes the diaphragm, the gap changes, and the capacitance follows the gap.

items: The diaphragm moves towards the back plate.
The charge or voltage on the plates changes, and the preamplifier gives an output.
On the opposite half-cycle the diaphragm moves away, the gap increases and C decreases; the output follows the sound waveform.

blocks.where: C is capacitance in farads (F); ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m is the permittivity of free space; A is the overlapping plate area in square metres (m²); d is the gap in metres (m).

ΔC is the change in capacitance in F; C is the initial capacitance in F; x is the diaphragm deflection towards the fixed plate in m; d is the initial gap in m. This small-change approximation holds when x is much smaller than d.

blocks.text: The back plate has holes or slots so air can move. Without holes, trapped air would resist the diaphragm and reduce sensitivity. The diaphragm must be thin and tight, like a drum skin, so small sound pressures produce motion.

A simple capacitor microphone needs a steady polarising voltage Vp across the plates. The charge is Q = C Vp. When C changes, charge must move, and a charge amplifier measures that charge. An electret microphone replaces the external supply with a permanent charge in a polymer layer. It still needs a high-impedance preamplifier. Electret capsules are the usual pick-up in electronic stethoscopes and phonocardiographs, which record heart sounds.

sections.h3: Signal conditioning, response and practical limits

blocks.text: The capacitance change is tiny, so the preamplifier decides performance. Two modes are used, and they behave differently.

Charge amplifier mode: the input is a virtual ground, and the feedback capacitor Cf collects the charge. With the input near zero volts, the cable capacitance carries almost no signal voltage and does not change the output. It still affects noise and stability, so keep the cable short and quiet.

Voltage preamplifier mode: the input impedance must be very high. The cable capacitance now adds in parallel with the microphone capacitance and forms a divider, so a long cable reduces the signal at the amplifier. Put a buffer or the preamplifier itself at the microphone.

blocks.where: Vout is the output voltage magnitude in V; Vp is the polarising voltage in V; ΔC is the capacitance change in F; Cf is the feedback capacitor in F.

items: Flat frequency response over a wide audio band.
Small diaphragms give good high-frequency and transient response; sensitivity rises with diaphragm area, so large diaphragms are more sensitive but roll off sooner.
Low noise with a good preamplifier.
Very high input impedance in voltage mode.
Cable capacitance matters in voltage mode; a charge amplifier is largely immune.

blocks.text: A capacitive pressure sensor uses a diaphragm as one plate and a fixed plate or deposited electrode as the other. Pressure on one side deflects the diaphragm, the gap changes and C changes. Signal conditioning converts ΔC to a voltage or a digital reading.

blocks.where: x is the pressure-driven deflection in m; d is the undeflected gap in m; A is the plate area in m²; ε₀ is the permittivity of free space in F/m.

blocks.text: For small deflection ΔC/C ≈ x/d, as in the microphone. For large deflection the denominator d − x changes a lot, the response becomes nonlinear, and calibration or linearisation is needed.

Three forms exist. An absolute sensor has a sealed vacuum reference on one side. A gauge sensor vents to atmosphere on one side. A differential sensor has two pressure ports and measures their difference. Capacitive sensors suit low-pressure and differential work because a small gap change gives a usable capacitance change: airway pressure in ventilators (0 to about 100 cmH<sub>2</sub>O), and flow from the pressure drop across a restrictor in spirometers.
Thin diaphragms and small gaps give sensitivity but make the sensor delicate. Overpressure can touch the plates or bend the diaphragm permanently. Mechanical stops and a careful housing protect it.

examples.question: A capacitor microphone has diaphragm area A = 25 mm², gap d = 20 μm, and relative permittivity εr = 1. Find C. A sound pressure moves the diaphragm by 0.020 μm towards the back plate. Find the new gap, the new C, the change in C, and the percentage change in C.
steps: Convert the area: A = 25 mm² = 25 × 10⁻⁶ m².
Convert the gap: d = 20 μm = 20 × 10⁻⁶ m.
Motion and permittivity: x = 0.020 μm = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ m; εr = 1, so ε = ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m.
New gap: d′ = d − x = 19.98 μm.
Change in capacitance: ΔC = C′ − C = 0.01108 pF.
examples.answer: C = 11.07 pF; new gap = 19.98 μm; new C = 11.08 pF; change = 0.011 pF; percentage change = 0.1001%.

examples.question: A ventilator airway-pressure sensor is modelled as a flat plate moving as a piston: A = 4 mm², d = 5.0 µm, deflection 0.02 µm per cmH<sub>2</sub>O, read by a charge amplifier with V<sub>p</sub> = 5 V and C<sub>f</sub> = 10 pF. Find C at 0, 20 and 100 cmH<sub>2</sub>O, the output at each, and the error of the small-change formula.
steps: 20 cmH<sub>2</sub>O: x = 0.40 µm, d − x = 4.60 µm, C = 7.699 pF, ΔC = 0.616 pF. Small-change estimate C₀·x/d = 7.083 × 0.08 = 0.567 pF, 8 % low.
100 cmH<sub>2</sub>O: x = 2.0 µm, d − x = 3.0 µm, C = 11.805 pF, ΔC = 4.722 pF; output 5 × 4.722/10 = 2.361 V. The small-change estimate 2.833 pF is 40 % low.
So 100 cmH<sub>2</sub>O gives 7.7 times the 20 cmH<sub>2</sub>O output for 5 times the pressure: the sensor must be linearised or kept to a small fraction of d.
examples.answer: 7.083, 7.699 and 11.805 pF; outputs 0, 0.308 and 2.361 V; the small-change formula is 8 % low at 20 and 40 % low at 100 cmH<sub>2</sub>O.

traps: Connecting a capacitor microphone straight to a low-impedance amplifier. It needs a charge amplifier or a very high input impedance, or the signal collapses.

Ignoring cable capacitance in a voltage-preamplifier design. The cable adds capacitance in parallel, divides the signal, and can make two identical microphones read differently. A charge amplifier at the microphone avoids this.
Mixing electret and externally polarised microphones. An electret has a permanent charge; a plain capacitor microphone needs a polarising supply.
Confusing absolute, gauge and differential pressure ports. A sealed vacuum reference, a vent to atmosphere, and two pressure ports are not interchangeable.
Using the small-change formula for large diaphragm deflection. C = ε₀A/(d − x) becomes nonlinear when x is a large fraction of d.

quiz.q: What changes inside a capacitor microphone when sound arrives?
quiz.a: The diaphragm moves, so the gap d changes. The capacitance C changes according to C = ε₀A/d.

quiz.q: Why does a plain capacitor microphone need a polarising voltage or an electret?
quiz.a: It needs steady charge on the plates. With polarising voltage Vp, charge Q = C Vp changes when C changes. An electret supplies a permanent charge instead.

quiz.q: A capacitive pressure sensor has C = 50 pF at d = 10 μm. Pressure reduces the gap by 0.10 μm. Use the small-change formula to find the percentage change in C and the new C.
In a voltage-preamplifier design, why can a long cable lower the sensitivity of a capacitor microphone?
quiz.a: The cable capacitance adds in parallel with the microphone capacitance and forms a divider with it, so less signal voltage reaches the amplifier. A buffer or the preamplifier at the microphone avoids this. A charge amplifier is not affected the same way, because its input is a virtual ground and carries almost no signal voltage.

quiz.q: Distinguish absolute, gauge and differential capacitive pressure sensors.
quiz.a: Absolute: one side is a sealed vacuum reference. Gauge: one side vents to atmosphere. Differential: two pressure ports, and the output depends on the pressure difference.

quiz.q: Why does a capacitive pressure sensor become nonlinear for large diaphragm deflection?
quiz.a: C = ε₀A/(d − x). For small x, ΔC/C ≈ x/d is nearly linear. For large x, the denominator changes strongly, so C rises faster than a straight line.

quiz.q: A capacitor microphone has C = 10 pF and a polarising voltage of 100 V. A sound changes C by 0.01 pF. Find the charge change.

beyond: Not for the exam. Phone microphones are mostly MEMS capacitive microphones, with the diaphragm and back plate etched on a silicon chip; capacitive pressure dies are built the same way. Search terms: MEMS capacitive microphone, electret microphone, charge amplifier, capacitive differential pressure sensor.
